Why pilots stall

Four ways AI programmes die. None of them is the model.

Your AI didn’t fail because the model was dumb. It failed because nobody owned it, the data wasn’t ready, legal turned up late and nobody changed how the work gets done. All four are fixable. None of them by buying another licence.

Failure mode 01

Nobody owns the outcome

AI sits between IT, operations and risk. Each assumes another is accountable, so pilots multiply without a business owner or a P&L target.

The fix: A named executive owner, a use-case portfolio with funding gates, and a monthly decision rhythm.

Failure mode 02

No data foundation

Pilots succeed on a hand-picked dataset and fail on production data that is fragmented, undocumented or not cleared for AI use.

The fix: A data-readiness check per use case before anything is built, and a register of permitted uses.

Failure mode 03

Governance arrives after the fact

Risk and legal review happen at the end, so promising pilots stall at the gate or ship without the controls customers and regulators now expect.

The fix: Risk tiers and human-in-the-loop controls designed in from day one, mapped to ISO/IEC 42001, the EU AI Act and NIST.

Failure mode 04

Adoption is left to chance

The tool works but the workflow never changed. Usage stays low, shadow tools fill the gap, and the benefit never shows up in the numbers.

The fix: Workflow redesign, training and targeted behaviour-change interventions, measured on usage and outcomes.

Your options

Four ways to get AI leadership. One of them is me.

An honest comparison, including the rows where I lose. Short definitions first, then the table.

What is an AI readiness assessment?

A structured evaluation of whether an organisation has the strategy, data, technology, people, governance and change capacity to adopt and scale AI. It ends with a scored map, a ranked use-case list and a roadmap, usually in two to four weeks.

Read the guide →

What is AI governance?

The policies, roles, risk controls and evidence that let an organisation use AI safely and prove it to boards, customers and regulators. It is usually built once, then mapped to ISO/IEC 42001, the EU AI Act and NIST AI RMF.

Read the guide →

What is a fractional Chief AI Officer?

A senior AI executive engaged part-time on retainer to own strategy, governance and vendor decisions without a full-time hire. It suits organisations that need AI leadership now but aren't ready for a permanent seat.

Read the guide →

When I'm not the right fit

If you need a 500-person delivery programme, a certified auditor, legal advice, or a vendor to run one specific platform, I'll say so on the first call and, where I can, point you to who can help.

Governance & Responsible AI

Governance isn’t a policy PDF. It’s the lock on the fridge.

Enterprise buyers, regulators and insurers keep asking one question: how do you govern your AI? “We have a policy somewhere” is not an answer. Evidence is. Organisations that can show it close deals, pass reviews and scale pilots without a legal handbrake.

I build governance that your teams will actually use: clear ownership, risk tiers, human oversight and a record you can show an auditor, then map it to the frameworks relevant to where you operate.

Published thinking. Co-author of “Empowering Ethical Artificial Intelligence Adoption: Bridging the Gaps with Ethics4AI”, on responsible technology adoption frameworks and AI governance.
